name: Hydroquinone-tretinoin-steroid triple cream (Kligman formula)

card.summary: The classic prescription melasma cream combining hydroquinone, tretinoin and a corticosteroid; the best-studied topical for the condition, with trials mostly run on branded Tri-Luma.
card.aka: Kligman formula, triple combination cream, Tri-Luma (fluocinolone/hydroquinone/tretinoin)
card.note: Prescription product; hydroquinone has been restricted by regulators, and a published 12-month study examined long-term use under supervision.

quick.overview:
The triple cream combines a skin-lightening agent (hydroquinone), a retinoid (tretinoin) and a topical steroid in one cream. It was devised in the 1970s by dermatologist Albert Kligman and is the standard topical for melasma, a chronic brown or grey facial pigmentation.
The branded fluocinolone version, Tri-Luma, has been tested in multicentre trials, and review articles describe it as more effective than hydroquinone alone. It is used to treat pigment disorders rather than to lighten normal skin.
quick.mechanism: Hydroquinone inhibits tyrosinase, the enzyme that makes melanin. Tretinoin speeds skin turnover and aids penetration, and the steroid reduces irritation and inflammation from the other two. Together they are described as complementary.
quick.risks: Reported effects include local irritation, and long-term steroid and hydroquinone use are the concerns reviewers raise. The 12-month open-label study of the fluocinolone version reported a favourable safety profile. Hydroquinone regulation is tightening: in the US over-the-counter products were banned in 2020, and tretinoin should be avoided in pregnancy.

lead: The hydroquinone-tretinoin-steroid triple combination cream, often called the Kligman formula, is a topical prescription treatment for melasma and other hyperpigmentation. It combines the skin-lightening agent hydroquinone, the retinoid tretinoin and a corticosteroid.[1][2]

Hydroquinone use for hyperpigmentation was reported from 1936, and in 1975 dermatologist Albert Kligman tested a combination of 5 percent hydroquinone, 0.1 percent tretinoin and 0.1 percent dexamethasone for melasma.[3] A stable once-daily commercial formulation containing 4 percent hydroquinone, 0.05 percent tretinoin and 0.01 percent fluocinolone acetonide (Tri-Luma) was later tested in multicentre trials, which reviews describe as showing greater efficacy than its single components.[1][2]

General references report that the triple combination works better than dual therapy or hydroquinone alone, while also noting that melasma treatments often prove unsatisfying and that recurrence is common after sun exposure.[4]

The ingredients are described as complementary. Hydroquinone reduces melanin synthesis, tretinoin accelerates epidermal turnover, and the corticosteroid limits irritation from the other two.[2][4] The formula also serves as the comparison arm for newer approaches such as topical metformin, cysteamine, tranexamic acid, microneedling and lasers, and a 2024 meta-analysis introduces Kligman's formulation as the gold standard treatment for melasma.[27][24][21]

paras: Melasma is a chronic, relapsing disorder of facial hyperpigmentation that is more common in women and in people with darker skin types. Hydroquinone is the best-known topical, with 2 percent available over the counter and 4 percent by prescription in some countries, and the triple combination is used as a first-line option.[4]

Expert commentary on melasma and post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation has also summarised management options, including combinations, sun protection and procedures.[5] The formulation has been tried in other conditions, including solar lentigines, post-sclerotherapy hyperpigmentation and, in a 2026 case report, a congenital epidermal nevus.[6][7]

Melasma presents as symmetrical brown or grey patches, mostly on the cheeks, forehead and upper lip. A 2011 review notes that about 90 percent of those affected are women and that it is more common in Fitzpatrick skin types IV to VI, with sun exposure and genetics the most important triggers and hormones playing a larger role in women.[28] The same review lists fixed triple or dual combinations containing hydroquinone, tretinoin, corticosteroids or azelaic acid as main approaches, used with UVA- and UVB-blocking sunscreen, and calls the modified Kligman formula very effective, particularly in epidermal melasma.[28]

The formula is also used for post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation, and a registered 2022 trial (n=66) tested brightening cream with lasers for post-sclerotherapy hyperpigmentation.[5][19] Reviews describe dyschromia as a leading reason for cosmetic consultation, particularly in people of diverse skin types.[5]

A 12-month, multicentre, open-label study of the fluocinolone/hydroquinone/tretinoin cream enrolled 228 patients with facial melasma; 76 percent completed it, most patients had one or two treatment courses of about six months, and the authors reported a favourable safety profile.[1]

A comprehensive review of short- and long-term use described the cream as a stable, once-daily formulation of three established monotherapies for a condition that is hard to treat in darker complexions.[2] A cost-effectiveness analysis compared the fixed combination with hydroquinone alone applied twice daily in several countries using data from an 8-week trial.[8]

A 2025 randomised, single-centre, placebo-controlled trial compared a generic fluocinolone/hydroquinone/tretinoin cream with Tri-Luma in Chinese patients with moderate-to-severe melasma.[9] A 2022 randomised trial compared oral tranexamic acid plus the fluocinolone-based triple cream with the cream alone.[10]

Comparative trials often use the formula as the reference treatment. A randomised study in Hamadan, Iran, of 42 women with facial melasma compared subepidermal triamcinolone injections with Kligman's formula over eight weeks, and MASI scores fell in both groups.[23] A randomised trial of 40 patients compared 30 percent topical metformin with the triple cream over eight weeks using the Melasma Area and Severity Index; both arms improved, with a mean MASI reduction of about 56 percent reported in the metformin group.[24] A 2026 split-face study compared topical metformin with the Kligman formula,[25] and a 2022 split-face trial of 20 women examined fractional Er:YAG laser added to the formula versus the formula alone.[20] A four-arm assessor-blinded trial of 50 patients combined the modified formula with microneedling and tranexamic acid and followed outcomes for six months.[21]

Cysteamine 5 percent has been compared with the modified formula in a double-blind randomised trial of epidermal melasma, and a 2024 meta-analysis of cysteamine trials frames it as a treatment studied in patients resistant to Kligman's formulation.[26][27]

The original Kligman formula of 1975 used 5 percent hydroquinone, 0.1 percent tretinoin and 0.1 percent dexamethasone.[16][3] Clinicians and trials commonly refer to a modified Kligman formula, and the term triple combination cream covers pharmacy-compounded versions as well as the branded fixed combination Tri-Luma (fluocinolone acetonide 0.01 percent, hydroquinone 4 percent, tretinoin 0.05 percent), applied once daily.[1][2][28]

Registered trials vary the steroid, for example mometasone furoate in place of fluocinolone, or compare the triple cream with the Westerhoff formula.[12][13] Other studies use the formula as a base to which a device or second agent is added, such as an Er:YAG laser, microneedling with topical tranexamic acid, or oral tranexamic acid.[20][21][10]

Topical steroids and retinoids both have skin effects, and a registered study (completed 2006, n=70) examined the atrophogenic potential of the triple cream for melasma.[11] Tretinoin should be avoided in pregnancy.[4]

Hydroquinone has been the subject of safety concerns: encyclopedic sources report rat studies showing increased tumour rates, and the US FDA banned over-the-counter use in 2020, saying it could not rule out a carcinogenic potential.[3]

Exogenous ochronosis, a blue-black or brown-grey pigmentation that can be mistaken for melasma, is the best-known concern with prolonged hydroquinone use. Wikipedia reports it was first described in 1975 and usually follows years of use, while a 2021 review concluded that risk is low at concentrations of 5 percent or less for limited periods with regular monitoring.[17][18] The 2024 cysteamine meta-analysis likewise says long-term use of Kligman's formulation is limited by that risk.[27] Regulators have acted at different points: Wikipedia states the EU has banned hydroquinone in cosmetic creams since 2000, and the US FDA revoked its generally-recognised-as-safe status in 2006 and banned over-the-counter products in 2020.[17][3]

The corticosteroid brings the usual concerns of topical steroids on facial skin, such as thinning, which prompted the registered atrophogenic-potential study.[11] Post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation was recorded as an adverse event in a 2024 randomised trial of the modified formula with microneedling.[21] Wikipedia notes tretinoin is contraindicated in pregnancy because of birth-defect risk.[29]

Hydroquinone inhibits tyrosinase and is a reducing agent and antioxidant.[3][4] Tretinoin speeds skin cell turnover, and the corticosteroid component is intended to limit irritation from the others.[2][4]

Albert Kligman (1916-2010) trained in botany and medicine at the University of Pennsylvania and, with James Fulton and Gerd Plewig, identified tretinoin as a treatment for acne and wrinkles, marketed as Retin-A; the FDA approved it for acne in 1971.[16][29] Hydroquinone's skin-lightening effect was reported in 1936, and in 1975 Kligman tested his combination of 5 percent hydroquinone, 0.1 percent tretinoin and 0.1 percent dexamethasone for melasma and related conditions.[3]

The formula spread as the Kligman formula and, later, modified versions with other steroids. A stable once-daily commercial version with fluocinolone acetonide went through multicentre trials and a 12-month safety study published in 2005, followed by a 2006 review and a 2007 cost-effectiveness analysis.[1][2][8] Regulatory change around hydroquinone continued: the FDA classified it as generally recognised as safe and effective in 1982, revoked that in 2006 and banned over-the-counter use in 2020.[3]

Kligman is also known for the research he ran at Holmesburg Prison from 1951 to 1974, including early human tests of tretinoin; a later lawsuit was dismissed on limitation grounds and the episode contributed to federal rules restricting prison research.[16][29]

Registered trials compare the triple cream with alternatives or add-ons: mometasone-based versions, the Westerhoff formula, topical metformin, oral tranexamic acid, microneedling and platelet-rich plasma.[12][13][14][15] Their results have not yet been published.
Published comparisons now include topical metformin, cysteamine, tranexamic acid, laser and microneedling, with the Kligman formula usually the control arm.[20][21][24][26]

The 2005 12-month study of 228 patients and the 2025 randomised trial against Tri-Luma in Chinese patients are the principal studies of the fluocinolone version.[1][9] A 2022 randomised trial examined oral tranexamic acid with the cream, and a 2007 analysis examined cost-effectiveness against hydroquinone alone.[8][10] A trial listing for solar lentigines (2008, n=22) is also registered.[6]

Other randomised trials use the Kligman formula as comparator: triamcinolone injections (2016, n=42), topical metformin 30 percent (2022, n=40), fractional Er:YAG laser added to the formula (2022, n=20 split-face), microneedling with tranexamic acid (2024, n=50), cysteamine 5 percent, and oral tranexamic acid versus modified Kligman formula versus placebo cream (2024).[23][24][20][21][26][22]

timeline.event: Hydroquinone first obtained from quinic acid.[3]
Skin-lightening effect of hydroquinone first reported.[3]
FDA approves tretinoin (Retin-A) for acne, based on work by Kligman and Fulton.[29]
Kligman tests hydroquinone, tretinoin and dexamethasone for melasma; hydroquinone-induced exogenous ochronosis is first described the same year.[3][17]
FDA classifies hydroquinone as generally recognised as safe and effective.[3]
EU bans hydroquinone in cosmetic creams.[17]
12-month open-label study of fluocinolone/hydroquinone/tretinoin cream published.[1]
FDA revokes its 1982 classification of hydroquinone.[3]
Review states ochronosis risk is low at 5% or less for limited periods with monitoring.[18]
Randomised trial compares a generic triple cream with Tri-Luma in Chinese patients.[9]

chain: Hydroquinone slows melanin production, tretinoin speeds cell turnover, a steroid calms irritation
Brown or grey facial patches fade over weeks to months
angle.text: People with melasma and other stubborn facial hyperpigmentation use the cream under a dermatologist's direction to lighten dark patches so the complexion looks more even. It is aimed at pigment disorders, and patches commonly return with sun exposure, so it is typically paired with sun protection.
